content: All individuals diagnosed with hepatitis B or C should have access to treatment and care services tailored to their specific health needs, preferences, and expectations. This approach ensures that care is person-centered and community-focused. For hepatitis B, monitoring should be longitudinal, allowing for continuous tracking of patients as they access treatment and care services. If necessary, patients should be re-engaged in care and treatment restarted. Those receiving hepatitis B treatment should also have the opportunity to monitor viral load suppression annually, provided HBV DNA testing is available. For hepatitis C, it is essential to document the completion of treatment and confirm cure through testing with HCV RNA (PCR) or HCV core antigen. Monitoring of patients with chronic viral hepatitis should be integrated with systems tracking other related health conditions, such as HIV, sexually transmitted infections, and tuberculosis. This integration is particularly critical in settings where chronic hepatitis treatment is initiated or maintained, including maternal, newborn, and child health services, as well as ART and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) sites. In the long term, countries should aim to integrate chronic hepatitis patient monitoring systems with those used for other conditions, such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and diabetes. These systems should also be linked with databases monitoring hepatitis-related complications, such as liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), as well as death registries. Ideally, all these databases should be interconnected and integrated into the broader health information system. This integration is vital for tracking progress and collecting data necessary for validating the elimination of viral hepatitis. A template patient management card, available in both paper and electronic formats, can be used to document and promote best practices in healthcare facilities. Consolidated guidelines on person-centered viral hepatitis strategic information emphasize the use of data to support the scaling up of hepatitis prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services. A minimum data set, containing essential demographic, clinical, and laboratory information, should be standardized and used to monitor patients and programs effectively. This data set captures key interactions along the cascade of prevention, testing, treatment, and related services, enabling the generation of core indicators for program monitoring and individual patient care. The minimum data set should include demographic details (e.g., unique identifier, name, sex, date of birth, contact information), hepatitis testing and diagnosis data (e.g., HBV and HCV test dates and results), comorbidities and risk factors (e.g., injecting drug use, alcohol consumption, pregnancy status, HIV status), treatment initiation and continuation details (e.g., treatment start dates, regimens prescribed, treatment interruptions), and data on hepatitis-related complications (e.g., liver cancer evaluations, death records). By aligning and linking these data elements to core indicators, countries can improve both patient care and program monitoring. Countries are encouraged to embed hepatitis surveillance planning within existing national health sector strategies and align it with monitoring and review processes. A stepwise approach is recommended for establishing data systems for viral hepatitis, depending on the maturity of the country’s information system. In the initial phase, hepatitis prevalence surveys and individual testing data from testing centers should be collected to estimate the burden of chronic hepatitis B and C. These data should be validated to establish a baseline for disease burden and prioritize interventions. In subsequent phases, person-centered routine program data should be used to manage and monitor testing and treatment coverage. These data systems should be supplemented with drug consumption data to validate the number of individuals treated. Countries should assess the availability, quality, and accessibility of existing data and develop a clear framework for data collection, integration, and analysis. Biomarker surveys are the most robust method for estimating the prevalence of chronic hepatitis B and C in the population. These surveys can be integrated into existing population-based surveys, such as Demographic and Health Surveys or HIV Impact Assessments. Surveys among specific groups, such as antenatal care attendees, blood donors, and key populations (e.g., people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, sex workers, prisoners), can provide valuable information on risk behaviors and infection prevalence. Routine testing data, such as those collected for blood donation or antenatal care, can also be analyzed to estimate infection rates and disease burden. Interoperability of data systems and the use of unique identifiers are essential for linking individual records, minimizing duplication, and enabling data exchange across different sources and systems. Unique identifiers, which are anonymous alphanumeric codes, can replace personal information to protect privacy while allowing individuals to access health services across facilities and programs. Countries should invest in secure and confidential data systems, protected by policies and rights, to ensure data security and prevent misuse. WHO encourages the sharing of person-centered data for public health purposes, provided it is done with patient consent, safeguards privacy, and ensures secure digital systems. Ultimately, integrating various data sources with unique identifiers and ensuring interoperability allows for automated analysis and aggregation of individual data. This approach minimizes duplication and enables the calculation of core indicators along the care cascade, which can be reported at the national level and to WHO through the Global Hepatitis Reporting System. Ensuring data confidentiality and security is a prerequisite, as healthcare data often include sensitive personal information that could lead to stigmatization or discrimination. Countries should develop transparent data governance frameworks to enable the secure exchange and use of health data.
